summary: Choose two vertical lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water; return that maximum area.
mainInsight: Area = width x min(height). Start with the widest container and always move the shorter wall inward: keeping the shorter wall can only give smaller area (width shrinks, height is still capped by it), so it is safe to discard.

approaches.name: Two pointers (move the shorter wall)
approaches.summary: l=0, r=n-1; record area; advance the pointer at the shorter line.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal; the justification in your comments (discarding the shorter wall) is exactly the proof.

promptVariants: Which technique solves Container With Most Water in O(n)?
What pattern fits 'maximise a function of two endpoints'?
options: Two pointers moving inward, always advancing the shorter wall
Sliding window of fixed size that moves across the heights array
Prefix sums of the heights to compute the water between two bars
Dynamic programming over every pair of left and right walls
cards.answer: Two pointers moving inward, always advancing the shorter wall
cards.explanation: Starting with maximum width and shrinking while discarding provably worse candidates.

promptVariants: Why is it safe to move the pointer at the SHORTER wall?
Prove why discarding the shorter wall loses nothing.
cards.answer: Any container using the shorter wall with a closer partner has smaller width and its height is still limited by that same shorter wall, so its area is <= the area just recorded. So the shorter wall can never be part of a better container and can be discarded.
keyPoints: Height capped by the shorter wall
cards.explanation: Moving the taller wall could only lose width without raising the cap.

promptVariants: What happens when both walls have the same height?
Which pointer should move on a tie?
options: Either may move; keeping both cannot beat the current area
Neither pointer moves, because the current area is already the best
Both pointers must move inwards together to avoid repeating a pair
Only the taller wall should move, since the shorter caps the area
cards.answer: Either may move; keeping both cannot beat the current area
cards.explanation: Any better container must exclude both walls because both cap the height equally; moving one (as your `>=` branch does) is enough since the other moves next iteration.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Both pointers must move inwards together: Not needed; moving one is safe.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the two-pointer solution: ___
Container With Most Water converges in ___ time.
cards.explanation: Each step moves one pointer inward.

promptVariants: The converging-pointer solution uses ___ extra space.
cards.explanation: Only l, r and the running max.

promptVariants: Why does the loop only need `l < r` and why is the first area `(r - l) * min(...)` always the widest candidate?
cards.answer: The starting pair has the maximum possible width, so every later pair is narrower and must compensate with a greater min height. l < r keeps two distinct walls. ans = -1 is merely a sentinel: areas are >= 0, so the first iteration overwrites it (0 would be cleaner).
cards.explanation: Initialising with 0 is the idiomatic choice.
